title: Directions and transport
goal: Ask the way, ride the LRT and buses, and give directions to a Grab driver — with the Malaysian road vocabulary you'll see on every sign.
bekal: open a question to a stranger with *tumpang tanya*
give and follow directions: turn, straight on, junction, roundabout
name Malaysian transport without mixing up the false friends

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Lost in Kuala Lumpur
dialogs.intro: Sarah got off at the wrong station and is now standing at a junction, holding a phone with an almost dead battery.

notes: **Tumpang tanya** ("may I borrow a question") is the standard opener when asking a stranger — like "excuse me, can I ask…". It's the first phrase to learn before you leave the house in Malaysia. A more formal alternative: *Maaf, boleh saya tanya?*
**Lepas tu** = after that, then. It's the most common sentence linker in Malaysian conversation. *Lepas tu belok kiri* = "then turn left".
**Lampu isyarat** ("signal lights") = traffic lights. That's the official term; people also just say *traffic light*.
**Tambang** = fare — for buses, taxis and ferries. *Berapa tambang?* = How much is the fare?

**Dalam** before a number means **about, around**. *Dalam dua ratus meter* = about two hundred meters, *dalam pukul tiga* = around three o'clock. Normally *dalam* means "in, inside", so this can puzzle you at first.

grammars.title: Giving directions
body: Directions in Malay are simple: a verb, then left or right. This table covers almost everything you'll need.
after: ⚠️ **Pusing balik** means **turn back, make a U-turn** — the most common use of *pusing* in Malaysia, and Grab drivers will say it to you. (In Indonesian *pusing* means dizzy; for a headache in Malay, say **pening**.)
Position words: **di depan** (in front of), **di belakang** (behind), **di sebelah** (next to), **di tepi** (beside, at the edge of), **berhampiran** (near) and **bertentangan dengan** (opposite).

blocks.text: Note **kapal terbang** ("flying ship") for a plane. On signs and official documents you'll also see *pesawat*, and both are fine.
**Touch 'n Go** is the card used for tolls and public transport in Malaysia, much like an Oyster card. Topping it up is **tambah nilai**, a phrase you'll see on every machine.

blocks.title: Phrases for a Grab or taxi driver
items: **Nak ke [tempat], boleh?** — Can you take me to …?
**Berapa tambang ke sana?** — How much is the fare there?
**Guna meter ya, bang.** — Use the meter, please.
**Boleh berhenti kat depan tu?** — Can you stop just up ahead?
**Saya kat pintu masuk utama.** — I'm at the main entrance.
**Lambat sikit tak apa.** — It's fine if we're a bit late.
**Jalan mana yang tak sesak?** — Which road isn't jammed?

head: Malay
English
rows: Follow this road to the end.

blocks.text: **Sesat** = lost. It also has a religious sense (*ajaran sesat* = heresy), but in everyday talk it's plain: *saya sesat* = I'm lost.
One more word for your collection: **jem** (from English *jam*). *Jalan jem* = the roads are jammed. Alternatives: *sesak*, *tersekat*.

items: Excuse me, where is the LRT station?
How much is the fare there?
Can you stop just up ahead?
